comments:
The majority of the information available on Phya pa has been provided in [EZ5JXHJY] and [8S7FDMCJ]. Summaries of the same are also found in [LQZU66YX]: 37-40, [F4UK2S8P]: 2-3, and [BW9UR427]: 35-36 (in French).


On his birth in 1109, the year of rNgog Blo ldan shes rab (ID:3786)'s passing, see [TM8DW8WA]: 32-33, [VKBZTBWN]: 4b4-5, and [8GL7ZT7Y]: 15b2-3.
On the date of his passing in a "sa mo glang" year, see [R894SIKE]: 400, [VKBZTBWN]: 4b4-5 and 6a5. 
[95UZA9Y5]: 40/3/5 (reported in [7FZ3B926]: 111 and [MPRU5QUC]: 206) specifies the day "sa mo glang gi lo'i nag pa zla ba nag po'i phyogs kyi tshes brgyad," i.e., on the 23rd of the third month.

A list of his students is provided in [EZ5JXHJY]: 356, based on [MQB8JGAX]: 297/4, [KL9XTQWI]: I, 454, [4YEPFBIB]: 340-341, [8GL7ZT7Y], fol. 15b3, [VKBZTBWN], fol. 4b7-5a4.
[FDEWZ2NZ]: 290 also mentions the list of the four "jo sras" from bSod nams dpal's Bla ma rngog pa yab sras rim par byon pa’i rnam thar rin po che’i rgyan gyi phreng ba.

'Gos lo tsa ba lists numerous works composed before Phya pa took the see of gSang phu; these include commentaries and summaries on the Five works of Maitreya, the Pramāṇaviniścaya, the Satyadvayavibhaṅga, Madhyamakālaṃkāra, Madhyamakāloka, and  Bodhicaryāvatāra. He mentions having seen these, the Yid kyi mun sel (ID:4503) and summaries on Madhyamaka, as well as (ID:4505) and (ID:5971). exX0032026-04-2304-02-58
'Gos lo tsa ba does not mention any composition dealing with monastic discipline. 

Śākya mchog ldan ([TM8DW8WA], 12-13 and 32) mentions a (doubtful) commentary on the Pramāṇavārttika (ID:3772) in addition to the commentary on the Pramāṇaviniścaya, and three summaries (small, intermediate, large), the intermediate one being the Yid kyi mun sel (ID:4503). (Discussed in [EZ5JXHJY]: 357, translated in [8S7FDMCJ]: 59).

Four groups of students are mentioned in Tibetan sources (which do not imply that the members of the respective groups were studying with Phya pa at the same time), with occasional variations:

1) The "Eight Great Lions" (seng chen brgyad). Eight scholars whose names contains the expression "seng ge," likely connoting their expertise in epistemology. The standard list includes gTsang nag pa (ID:3839), Dan 'bag (ID:3840), 'Bru sha (ID:3841), rMa bya (ID:3842), rTsags/rTsegs (ID:4289), Myang/Nyang bran (ID:3844), and gNyal pa/dMyal ma (ID:6679). The eighth one is instead sometimes said to be gTsang pa 'Jam dpal (ID:6336), 'U yug pa (ID:3846), or mTshur ston (DI:4315).

2) The "four sons of noble families" (jo sras mi bzhi) or the "three sons of noble families" (jo sras gsum). They are young noble men of the rNgog (ID:3847), 'Khon (ID:3848), Khu (ID:3849), and gNyos/sMyos (ID:3850). The four are listed in [VKBZTBWN]: 4a7 and [8GL7ZT7Y]: 15b3, whereas on 16a1 the author speaks of "jo sras gsum." The four are also listed by bSod nams dpal, see [FDEWZ2NZ]: 290.

3) The "three wise ones" (shes rab can mi gsum) or "four wise ones" (shes rab can mi bzhi). The threefold-list in [VKBZTBWN]: 5a1 has rKong po (ID:3852), lHo pa sgom gzan (ID:3853), Par bu ba/sPar phu ba (ID:3854). 'Gar dbang grub (ID:3851) is added in the fourfold list, e.g. in [R894SIKE]: 406.

4) The "three accomplished ones" (grub thob mi gsum). These are students who later became famous masters: Dus gsum mkhyen pa (ID:3855), Phag mo gru pa (ID:3856), gSal sto (ID:3857). The third is sometimes replaced by Zhang tshal (ID:6409), or is suggested to be the latter's direct student.
